title: AI Dev 26 x SF | Aman Singla & Aseem Chandra: MarcoPolo, A Workspace for AI to Work with Your Data

segments.text: My name is Aman Singla and I'm here on
behalf of the team building Marco Polo.
We are a small and mighty team but we
are on a mission to connect agentic AI
to enterprise data. By agentic AI I mean
tools like claude, chat, GPT, curser,
perplexity, any of the agentic AI tools
that you might be using or you might
even be building. Okay, your own agent
apps. And by enterprise data, I mean uh
data sitting in raw storage, databases,
data warehouses, systems of record like
CRM, support systems, ERP, etc. So
let's uh begin by kind of talking about
where we are today. We are all
developers uh you know engineers we know
coding agents actually work. We have
been using them in production. We have
been using them to put a lot of code
into production and uh you know they
have been phenomenal.
Uh we have MCPs uh coming online uh
hundreds and thousands of MCP servers
every day uh and APIs which are
connecting AI to real systems. But still
real work with real data is still hard
for anybody outside of developers.
Right? What I mean by real work with
real data are ops people like who are
adjusting to developers who are trying
to maybe build some automations or build
some dashboards and they're not working
with code directly but they're trying to
get their work done and that's kind the
kind of work where maybe you can do a
few demos but trying to do that kind of
work in production is really hard and
let's talk about it why why is it hard?
So let's use this example which is a
very simple example which essentially
says okay show me which of my customers
churned last quarter and pull their
support tickets. So this might be a
question which somebody in your revops
team might have or in your support ops
team might have now to you got
Salesforce MCP hooked up and yes
Salesforce MCP uh came online a couple
of weeks ago so we know that so they
hook up Salesforce MCP but it's got a
lot of tools it's got a lot of APIs. So
first your LLM is already got a lot of
context that it has to work through to
figure out the right tool to use. Maybe
it figures out that the right thing to
do in this case is to write SQL query
goes and gets you a list of the churn
accounts. But where is it pulling it?
It's pulling them into context. And now
its context is continuing to grow. Next,
now it needs to go figure out from Jira
the support tickets for these accounts.
Uh a couple of ways we as developers
might think about it as yeah, just
download the data from Jira and join it.
But maybe your AI doesn't know how to
join or doesn't have a place to join. So
it's going to now figure out whether to
write a JJQL query or use the APIs.
Maybe it will pull these accounts one by
one and try to make it work. But already
you know it's context is blowing up. It
doesn't have a place to do the join and
it's probably going to hallucinate a
solution for you. So how do we actually
solve this problem? So we have a very
simple thesis. Our thesis is that yes we
need MCP servers. We need APIs to
connect us to real data and real
systems. But more than that, now to make
that useful and to put that into
production, we need a workspace. See, if
your uh ops person was actually trying
to do this themselves, they would
probably be downloading the data from
Salesforce using an Excel file or a CSV
file. They would then be downloading the
data from Jira then putting it together
in Excel and they would be working in
this way. But what is that particular
workspace? Where does the AI get to work
and do that kind of work is really what
we mean by a workspace. So let's make it
more concrete. Okay, what does it really
mean? So what makes a real workspace?
Let's go over the three things we
believe are very critical to making a
workspace. One critical thing for us to
understand is this workspace concept is
not just being enforced through prompts
and suggestions to LLM. It is actually
being enforced by architecture. It's
just like when we work with code there
is you know a repo and there is a code
and structure and architecture etc.
There we are giving this shape uh so
that the LLM can actually effectively
work with your data. So that's the
architecture and the shape of the system
that we are talking about. So the first
thing you need is a place and tools for
it to do the work. Remember the example
of the ops user. So for him or her the
tools would have been to be able to
download the data and to be able to join
them in Excel. In our case what we do is
we take DB and put that beside the LLM
so that it has tools not just to
download the data but to load that up
into DB DB and actually do the join etc
there. So now it has real tools and a
real place to be able to do the work. So
that's one critical factor about having
a workspace. The second key thing is
context. Right? When you're working with
systems, you need to figure out what
data to use, how to use it, when to use
it. Now again, we as developers know how
to prompt the LLM into giving us the
right answer or the right information.
We can guide it. But a lot of times
people don't have the experience or the
understanding to be able to do that. So
you have a cold start problem where you
are trying to get the LLM to uh enough
information so that it can be effective
on a query. So it needs schema, it needs
some level of docs to be able to know
how to connect to Salesforce, what
syntax to use. So we get it started with
that and as it uses that information to
write queries and the context grows with
usage. So it becomes a learning system.
So that's the second thing that you need
in a workspace which is an ability for
context to be able to compound. And the
third critical thing why people are not
being able to work with their data
really is that uh you know the IT is
worried about security. Uh you know what
data is being exposed to the LLM? What
credentials are being exposed to the
LLM? Does it have the right access or
permissions for the task it needs to do?
So you need a security model which
actually controls and manages all that
so that your uh it can feel comfortable
with you working with the real data. So
that's the third critical problem that
uh workspace needs to be able to solve.
And one key thing is that the access you
have has to be tied to the context you
have because the access kind of
determines what kind of systems are you
allowed to work with and what can you do
with them and your context also follows
from that. So these are three things
which make a workspace very concrete.
Now one of the things I talked about in
the workspace was the tools that are
needed in the workspace and one of the
innovations we have done is we have
given it a single CLI a single tool to
work across 50 different data sources.
So it has these connections and each of
these connections has a scope but we
give it verbs like list, query,
describe, browse, upload, download for
it to be able to now work with these
connections through this one layer of
abstraction without really loading up a
lot of information and context about the
50 different tools that might be trying
to talk to. So it reduces the surface
for the agents and behind the scenes the
system actually multiplexes to storage
systems to databases to warehouses to
SAS applications to give this one
abstraction which allows the LLM to work
with them very effectively without
really trying to without growing its
context a lot. Okay, so that's one of
the key things and this is very very
effective in getting the LLM to perform
a lot better across a broad set of data
sources.
The next key thing which is very
critical is the context. Remember we
talked about the cold start problem
about when somebody is looking to query
Salesforce or looking to query a
database. uh the AI needs to know some
information about the schema, some
information about the syntax so that it
doesn't trip on its first set of queries
for it to be able to actually produce a
useful query for you quickly enough and
get you the right information that
you're looking for. So that's where when
we connect to a data source, we are able
to curate this information so that the
person using the tool can actually have
a good experience with the LM from day
one. But then the next critical thing is
as they continue using the tool, every
query is improving the next query. It's
a persistent workspace. So it's
remembering the queries that were made.
That information is very useful for
auditing, for going back and looking at
the queries, uh what got queried, what
data got exposed. But it's also very
useful for the LLM to be able to say,
"Ah, I wrote that query already. Let me
not waste tokens or writing a new one."
So it can reuse that query. And more
than that often it uses the queries
which are existing to understand the
relationships of across the data and
write better queries or the next query
uh writing the next query becomes very
easy for it. So it can remember joins it
can remember relationships and that
allows it to have enough context to as
you ask more sophisticated questions or
a different set of questions to have
that information to write the right
queries. Finally the this is the most
important part which is as these
workspaces and a lot of these workspaces
are provisioned per user. They might be
provisioned per agent. They might be
provisioned for a project where you know
you might have different people working
on a project and using the same
workspace. As these workspaces are
acrewing context these actually become a
aggregated knowledge base for the
company for the entire org. So these
workspaces now have collected
information which can be useful when
you're starting something new when
you're seeding a new workspace to be
able to look from that and you can have
that give a a new workspace a warm
start. So think about it pretty much
like onboarding a new employee. you
know, you give them a computer and you
have their buddy who actually helps them
set up the computer, hook it up to the
right systems and give it them the right
information about how to work with them
and what data exists in those systems.
So think about a similar process
happening when it is actually
aggregating knowledge for the org. Uh so
so this is how context gets built up and
this becomes a very critical asset for
the enterprise itself uh as a knowledge
base for the enterprise.
So to sum it up, let me kind of show you
an architecture diagram about how it all
comes together. So on the left you have
your agentic AI. So this could be
claude chat GPT cursor copilot etc.
or any agentic AI app that you have been
building. And on the right side is your
data. And and Marco Polo is the
middleware which runs in a secure
Kubernetes container. It's got
persistence for the workspace which is
the file system. So those two things
come together to give you a Marco Polo
workspace. We already talked about it
connects across 50 plus systems. It's
got schema. It's got context. It's got
duct TV tools runtime. So that this can
be effective container. The key thing I
want to touch upon here is actually the
scope credentials. So each workspace has
credentials which are scoped to the
workspace. They correspond to the
context in the workspace. They're
encrypted. They're managed to the file
system, but they're also not accessible
by the LLM. They're sitting in a
privilege access mode. So that the CLI I
kind of showed you is the one through
which they are being accessed by the LM
but the LLM can write any script or do
anything but it will not have direct
access to the LMS. It has to be able to
exercise those systems through this
interface that is provided to you. So
for those of you who understand Linux or
Unix and have been using those kind of
systems, it's kind of almost like a OS
level boundary that is available that
you can actually make privilege calls to
the OS to get it to do work on your
behalf, but you don't get access to the
underlying resources directly. So that's
the setup that Marco Polo has. Now let
me show you how this works in practice.
So you know what I have here is some uh
real traces around which I have actually
articulated how the uh claude went
through so that you can follow through
and you can understand if you want to
look through the real traces we are just
around the corner in that booth over

this particular talk about how the LM
worked on something. So let's start with

okay uh let's figure out the number of

as I said schema on connect to solve the
cold start problem in this particular
case the LM already knows that it has
through this workspace it can figure out
it's connected to seven different data
sources. it needs to talk to Salesforce
and it has the schema for Salesforce
available on the right side right here
and this is an actual asset in the
workspace that is available. So this is
the path of the asset at the bottom of
it. But because of this schema being
present it can actually understand that
Salesforce does not have an object

called type and within the type it can
go look for customers and b because of
that it was able to come back and say
hey I found 208 account objects but only
200 of them were tag customers and maybe
eight of them are missing some data or
there might be prospects which somebody
has not categorized. So this is the
level of a sophisticated response that
your ops team expects or if you had
given that problem to an analyst that's
the kind of response they would have
come back with versus just kind of
giving you running a random query and
giving you an answer like 208 because
that answer is not really meaningful to
you in this particular context. So
that's the schema unconnect so that you
can solve this cold short problem.
Let's do something more sophisticated
now. Let's actually ask the LLM to build

region. So this is a complicated query
which we are asking it to do and not

Let's see how the LM tackles this

it's got the right skills within the

here. And the third thing is it's

now this becomes makes the query uh
